written.q: Define a tree and explain root, leaf, subtree and order. What is a binary tree?
written.a: A tree is a set of nodes holding atomic or composite data, connected by edges. The root is the top node (no parent); a leaf is a node with no children; a subtree is a node with everything below it (itself a tree); the order is the maximum number of children a node can have. A binary tree has order two: a finite set of elements partitioned into a root, a left subtree and a right subtree, each of which is again a binary tree.

written.q: Describe preorder, inorder and postorder traversal and give the three results for a tree with root a, left child b (children c, d) and right child e (right child f).
written.a: Preorder: visit the root, traverse the left subtree in preorder, traverse the right subtree in preorder. Inorder: traverse the left subtree in inorder, visit the root, traverse the right subtree in inorder. Postorder: traverse left in postorder, right in postorder, then visit the root. Results: preorder a b c d e f; inorder c b d a e f; postorder c d b f e a.

written.q: Define a binary search tree. Store 70, 50, 30, 80, 60, 40, 20 in one using the recursive insert rule and give the preorder output. (Prototype question 3)
written.a: A BST is a binary tree in which every node of the left subtree is less than the root, every node of the right subtree is greater than or equal to the root, and every subtree is itself a BST. Rule: insert(number, node): if node is empty store the number; else if number < value in node, insert into the left child; else into the right child. Result: root 70; left 50 (left 30 with children 20 and 40; right 60); right 80. Preorder: 70, 50, 30, 20, 40, 60, 80. Inorder gives 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80.

written.q: Explain how a tree is stored in an array and list the problems of an array-based tree.
written.a: The root is at index 1; the node at index n has its left child at 2n and its right child at 2n + 1; 0 marks an empty slot. A tree of height h needs 2h+1 array elements for up to 2h+1 − 1 nodes, so an unbalanced tree wastes memory dramatically; the array cannot grow or shrink. It is fine if the tree is balanced or the maximum height is known and fixed. A linked list-based tree can grow and shrink.

written.q: Write the addNode and traverseInorder algorithms of a linked list-based tree.
written.a:
ALGORITHM addNode(REF p POINTER to node, VAL d DATATYPE)
1 IF (p = null)
2    p ← ALLOCATE MEMORY node
3    p->data ← d
4    p->left ← null
5    p->right ← null
6 ELSE
7    IF (d < p->data)
8       addNode(p->left, d)
9    ELSE
10      addNode(p->right, d)
11   END IF
12 END IF
END addNode

ALGORITHM traverseInorder(VAL p POINTER to node)
1 IF (p ≠ null)
2    traverseInorder(p->left)
3    PRINT(p->data)
4    traverseInorder(p->right)
5 END IF
END traverseInorder

written.q: Explain why a binary search tree implemented with a linked list is efficient for searching a large dynamic set of data, compared with an array and with a linked list.
written.a: Binary search on an array requires sorted data, so inserting or deleting forces shifting elements to keep it sorted. A linked list makes insertion and deletion efficient (only addresses change) but searching it is not efficient. A linked list-based BST combines both: insertion and removal only change addresses, and searching is fast because each comparison selects one subtree.

written.q: Draw the expression tree for 3 + 5 × 2 and give its three traversals.
written.a: Root +; left child 3; right child × with children 5 and 2 (the multiplication is below the addition because it is done first). Inorder: 3 + 5 × 2; preorder: + 3 × 5 2; postorder: 3 5 2 × +. The postfix form is evaluated with a stack: 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 + 10 = 13.
